title: Characteristics of Living Organisms
bodyMd:
# Characteristics of Living Organisms

## Characteristics of living organisms

> **Spec point** — `1.1.1` · (a) movement as an action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place
(b) respiration as the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism
(c) sensitivity as the ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment
(d) growth as a permanent increase in size and dry mass
(e) reproduction as the processes that make more of the same kind of organism
(f) excretion as the removal of the waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements
(g) nutrition as the taking in of materials for energy, growth and development

## Characteristics of living organisms

- All living organisms (animal, plant, fungus, prokaryote and protoctist) demonstrate the characteristics:

  - **movement**: an action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place
  - [respiration](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/12-respiration/12-1-respiration/12-1-1-respiration-in-cells/): the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism
  - **sensitivity**: the ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment
  - **growth**: a permanent increase in size and dry mass
  - **reproduction**: the processes that make more of the same kind of organism
  - [excretion](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/13-excretion-in-humans/13-1-excretion-in-humans/13-1-1-excretion-in-humans/): the removal of the waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements
  - **nutrition**: the taking in of materials for energy, growth and development

> **Exam Hint**
> You can use this mnemonic to help you remember the 7 characteristics that all living organisms demonstrate:
> 
> **MRS GREN**
> 
> - **M**ovement
> - **R**espiration
> - **S**ensitivity
> - **G**rowth
> - **R**eproduction
> - **E**xcretion
> - **N**utrition
> 
> Some common misconceptions to watch out for:
> 
> - Bacteria (a type of prokaryote) also show all of the characteristics listed above
> - Confusing the living characteristic **excretion** with **egstion**, which is the removal of undigested food from the body as faeces

title: Concept & Uses of Classification Systems
bodyMd:
# Concept & Uses of Classification Systems

## How organisms are classified

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_nP8zcNSRTzGnHzpZ` · State that organisms can be classified into groups by the features that they share
Describe a species as a group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring

## How organisms are classified

- There are millions of species of organisms on Earth
- A species is defined as a group of organisms that can **reproduce to produce fertile offspring**
- These species can be classified into groups by the [features that they share](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/1-characteristics-and-classification-of-living-organisms/1-1-characteristics-classification-and-features-of-organisms/1-1-4-features-of-organisms/)

## The binomial system

> **Spec point** — `1.2.3` · Describe the binomial system of naming species as an internationally agreed system in which the scientific name of an organism is made up of two parts showing the genus and species

## The binomial system

- Organisms were first classified by a Swedish naturalist called **Linnaeus** in a way that allows the subdivision of living organisms into smaller and more specialised groups
- The species in these groups have more and more features in common the more subdivided they get
- He named organisms in Latin using the **binomial system, **an internationally agreed system in which the scientific name of an organism is made up of two parts showing the **genus** and **species**

  - The **genus** name is capitalised and comes before the species name
  - The **species** name is not capitalised and follows the genus name

- When typed binomial names are always in **italics** (which indicates they are Latin) e.g. *Homo sapiens*
- The sequence of classification is: **Kingdom**, **Phylum**, **Class**, **Order**, **Family**, **Genus**, **Species**

![Diagram of Linnaeus’s classification from general to specific for Homo sapiens: kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Mammalia, order Primates, family Hominidae, genus Homo, species Homo sapiens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/00cfe8fa5e44-linnaeuss-system-of-classifcation.png)

*Linnaeus’s system of classification*

> **Exam Hint**
> The order of classification can be remembered by using a mnemonic like:
> 
> **K**ing **P**hilip **C**ame **O**ver **F**or **G**ran's **S**paghetti
> 
> You do need to know for a given name which part is the genus and which part is the species because you could be given an unfamiliar binomial name and asked for either of these.
> 
> For examples, the binomial name for the house mouse is *Mus musculus.* If you were asked to give the genus name for the house mouse, it would be *Mus.* If you were asked for the species name, it's *musculus.*

## Dichotomous keys

> **Spec point** — `1.2.4` · Construct and use dichotomous keys based on identifiable features

## Dichotomous keys

- Keys are used to identify organisms based on a **series of questions about their features**
- Dichotomous means ‘branching into two’ and it leads the user to identify the organism by giving **two descriptions at a time** and asking them to choose between them
- Each choice leads the user on to another two descriptions
- In order to successfully navigate a key you should:

  - Follow the statements from the beginning. Use the information or image provided in the question to answer the first statement, which will direct you to the next statement
  - Keep working through the key. If you are presented with a branching key, eventually there will be no statements left for the branch you have followed and you will have identified the organism. If you are presented with a key in a table format, you will be directed to a statement or given a name
- Fo branching keys, if you are given more than one organism to identify, it's vital that you **start at the beginning of the key for each organism**, repeating until all organisms are named

![Illustrated green leaf with toothed edge and veins, beside a flowchart-style identification key describing leaflet shapes and edges.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/3c6ef4b3e9b2-example-of-a-dichotomous-key-1.png)

*Example of a dichotomous key #1*

![Diagram titled “Five species of mollusc” showing labelled drawings A–E of different shells, a tentacled nautilus and an unsegmented slug with exam instructions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/fbb772fb2c69-example-of-dichotomous-key-2-part-1.png)

*Example of a dichotomous key #2*

| Key | Letter |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (a) | Body is completely or partly covered in a shell | Go to 2 |   |
| 1 (b) | Body is **not** completely or partly covered in a shell | *Limax Flavus* | **E** |
| 2 (a) | Shell is attached to rocks by thin threads | *Mytilus edulis* | **A** |
| 2 (b) | Shell is **not** attached to rocks by thin threads | Go to 3 |   |
| 3 (a) | Shell is a spire that comes to a point | *Buccinum undatum* | **C** |
| 3 (b) | Shell is **not** a spire that comes to a point | Go to 4 |   |
| 4 (a) | Animal has tentacles | *Nautilus pompilius* | **D** |
| 4 (b) | Animal has 2 tentacles | *Planorbis planorbis* | **B** |

> **Exam Hint**
> Simple dichotomous keys frequently come up in the multiple choice paper, so make sure you can use one. Very occasionally they show up in the theory paper. Questions usually ask you to use a key rather than construct one, so practise using them first. Be ready to construct a simple key though, as the syllabus asks for both

title: Concept & Uses of Classification Systems Continued
bodyMd:
# Concept & Uses of Classification Systems Continued

## Reflecting evolutionary relationships: Extended

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_bX9gHFfxmkGxVMfQ` · nan

## Reflecting evolutionary relationships: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

- Classification systems aim to **reflect evolutionary relationships** between species
- Traditional biological classification systems grouped organisms based on the **features** that they **shared**

  - If organisms shared more similar features then they were said to be more closely related
- In the past, scientists have encountered many **difficulties** when trying to determine the** evolutionary relationships** of species based on this method
- Using the physical features of species (such as colour/shape/size) has **many limitations** and can often lead to the **wrong classification** of species

## Using DNA to classify organisms: Extended

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_c3B2hSp4N4wGjTKm` · nan

## Using DNA to classify organisms: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

- Organisms share features because they originally descended from a **common ancestor**

  - Example: all mammals have bodies covered in hair, feed young from mammary glands and have external ears (pinnas)
- Originally, organisms were classified using **morphology** (the overall form and shape of the organism, e.g. whether it had wings or legs) and **anatomy** (the detailed body structure as determined by dissection)
- As technology advanced, **microscopes**, knowledge of **biochemistry** and eventually **DNA sequencing** allowed us to classify organisms using a more scientific approach
- Studies of DNA sequences of different species show that organisms sharing a more recent ancestor have more similar base sequences than those that share only a distant ancestor
- This means that the **base sequences in a mammal’s DNA are more closely related to all other mammals** than to any other vertebrate groups

![Diagram comparing five beetle species by coloured DNA base sequences, showing similarities and differences in nucleotide order across two gene regions.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/e70128953a92-dna-sequences-can-show-how-closely-related-diffe.png)

*DNA sequences can show how closely related different species are*

- The sequences above show that *Brachinus armiger* and *Brachinus hirsutus* are **more closely related** than any other species in the list as their DNA sequences are identical except for the last but one base (*Brachinus armiger* has a T in that position whereas *Brachinus hirsutus* has an A)
- As DNA base sequences are used to code for **amino acid sequences in proteins**, amino acid sequences can also be compared to determine how closely related organisms are - the more similar the sequence, the more closely related (and vice versa)

title: Features of Organisms
bodyMd:
# Features of Organisms ## The five kingdoms > **Spec point** — `1.3.1` · State the main features used to place animals and plants into the appropriate kingdoms ## Kingdoms: animals & plants - All living organisms share characteristics. Organisms can be grouped together based on common features they share - All living organisms can be grouped into one of five kingdoms - Animals and plants are both kingdoms within this grouping system - **Main features of all animals:** - they are multicellular - their cells contain a nucleus but no cell walls or chloroplasts - they feed on organic substances made by other living things ![Diagram of a typical animal cell labelled with nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria and ribosomes on rough endoplasmic reticulum](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/6336e7621ab4-a-typical-animal-cell.png) *A typical animal cell* - **Main features of all plants:** - they are multicellular - their cells contain a nucleus, chloroplasts and cellulose cell walls - they all feed by photosynthesis ![Diagram of a typical plant cell labelled with cell wall, cell membrane, chloroplasts, nucleus, mitochondria, cytoplasm, vacuole and rough ER with ribosomes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/bf31e104ae8e-a-typical-plant-cells.png) *A typical plant cell* ## The animal kingdom > **Spec point** — `1.3.2` · State the main features used to place organisms into groups within the animal kingdom, limited to: (a) the main groups of vertebrates: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish (b) the main groups of arthropods: myriapods, insects, arachnids, crustaceans Classify organisms using the features identified ## The animal kingdom - Several main features are used to [place organisms into groups](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/1-characteristics-and-classification-of-living-organisms/1-1-characteristics-classification-and-features-of-organisms/1-1-2-concept-and-uses-of-classification-systems/?_ai=internal-linking) within the animal kingdom ### Vertebrates - All vertebrates have a **backbone** - There are five classes of vertebrates #### Vertebrate table | Class | Main features | Examples | |---|---|---| | Mammals | - Fur/hair on skin
- Have a placenta
- Young feed on milk from mammary glands
- External ears (pinna) visible
- Endothermic | Horse, dog, squirrel, human | | Birds | - Skin covered in feathers
- Have 2 legs and 2 wings instead of forelimbs
- Lay eggs with hard shells on land
- Have a beak
- Endothermic | Parrot, blue tit, eagle | | Reptiles | - Dry, fixed scales on skin
- Lay eggs with rubbery shells on land | Snake, turtle, iguana | | Amphibians | - Smooth, moist skin
- Adults usually live on land (and so have lungs)
- Larvae live in water (and so have gills)
- Lay eggs without shells in water | Frog, toad, newt | | Fish | - Loose, wet scales on skin
- Use gills to breathe
- Lay eggs without shells in water | Flounder, grouper | ![Diagram showing vertebrate groups—reptiles, fish, amphibians, birds and mammals—with simple notes on skin, eggs, blood temperature and example animals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/b852310294dc-vertebrate-classifcation.png) *Vertebrate classification* ### Invertebrates - Invertebrates do not possess a backbone - One of the morphological characteristics used to classify invertebrates is **whether they have legs or not** - All invertebrates with **jointed legs** are part of the **arthropod** phylum - All arthropods share the following visible features: - They have an exoskeleton - They have a segmented body - They have jointed legs - They are classified further into the following groups: #### Arthropod groups table | Class | Main features | Examples | |---|---|---| | Myriapods | - Body consists of many segments
- Each segment contains at least one pair of jointed legs
- One pair of antennae | Centipede | | Insects | - Three-part body: head, thorax and abdomen
- Adults have six jointed legs
- Two pairs of wings (one or both pairs may be vestigial, meaning non-functional and undeveloped)
- One pair of antennae | Butterfly | | Arachnids | - Two-part body: cephalothorax and abdomen
- Four pairs of jointed legs
- No antennae | Spider | | Crustaceans | - More than four pairs of jointed legs
- Chalky exoskeleton formed from calcium
- Use gills to breathe
- Two pairs of antennae | Crab | ![Diagram showing classification of arthropods into arachnids, crustaceans, insects and myriapods, with simple drawings and key features of each group.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/fdb754bc8fb6-arthropod-classifcation.png) *Arthropod classification* > **Exam Hint** > - Make sure that you are aware of the distinction between the** main features **of a group of organisms and the **defining features** of a group: > - An exam question might ask you to state the *main* features of a group of organisms; these are given above, and some of these main features are **shared between the groups** > > - E.g. all of the vertebrates have a backbone, and all of the arthropods have segmented bodies > - It is also possible that an exam question might ask you to give a *defining* visible feature of any one of these groups, i.e. a feature that **sets a group apart from the other groups** > > - E.g. mammals have fur while the other vertebrates do not, and crustaceans have two pairs of antennae while this is not the case for the other groups of arthropods > - It is common for students to confuse arachnids with crustaceans, and to not be able to state a visible feature identifying an organism as an arthropod, any one of "exoskeleton, jointed legs or segmented body" would be an appropriate answer

title: Features of Organisms Continued
bodyMd:
# Features of Organisms Continued

## The five kingdoms: Extended

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_STGvsdh7n4HZmjr5` · nan

## The five kingdoms: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

- The first division of living things in the classification system is to put them into one of** **[five kingdoms](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/1-characteristics-and-classification-of-living-organisms/1-1-characteristics-classification-and-features-of-organisms/1-1-4-features-of-organisms/?_ai=internal-linking)
- They are:

  - Animals
  - Plants
  - Fungi
  - Protoctists
  - Prokaryotes
- The main features of animals and plants have already been covered on the [previous revision note](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/1-characteristics-and-classification-of-living-organisms/1-1-characteristics-classification-and-features-of-organisms/1-1-4-features-of-organisms/) page
- **Main features of all fungi (e.g. moulds, mushrooms, yeast)**

  - Usually **multicellular**
  - Cells have **nuclei** and **cell walls** not made from cellulose
  - Do not photosynthesise but **feed by saprophytic** (on dead or decaying material) **or parasitic** (on live material) **nutrition**

![Diagram of a basic fungal cell labelled with cell wall made of chitin, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion and ribosomes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/4000dc417c55-a-typical-fungal-cell.png)

*A typical fungal cell*

- **Main features of all Protoctists (e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium)**

  - **Most are unicellular,** but some are multicellular
  - All have a **nucleus**, some may have cell walls and chloroplasts
  - Meaning **some protoctists photosynthesise** and **some feed on organic substances** made by other living things

![Diagram comparing two protocist cells, labelling nucleus, ribosomes, food vacuoles, contractile vacuole, mitochondria, cytoplasm and cell membrane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/5133fc58b53c-two-examples-of-protoctist-cells.png)

*Two examples of protoctist cells*

> **Exam Hint**
> Protoctist is the kingdom that students are least likely to recall the features of, or identify from an image or description of, in an exam.
> 
> The key features are:
> 
> - Cells **always have a nucleus**
> - Organisms are **usually unicellular**, although some are multicellular
> 
>   - This is key difference, as other organisms formed from cells with a nucleus are often multicellular
> - **They have varied nutrition**: Some obtain nutrition like plants (by photosynthesising), while others act like fungi or animals (by consuming organic matter)

- **Main features of all Prokaryotes (e.g. bacteria, cyanobacteria)**

  - Often **unicellular**
  - Cells have **cell walls** (not made of cellulose) and **cytoplasm** but **no nucleus or mitochondria**

![Diagram of a typical bacterial cell labelled with cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA loop and plasmids, with flagella shown.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/1ea0a4eb3551-a-typical-bacterial-cell.png)

*A typical bacterial cell*

## The plant kingdom: Extended

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_vf7FFgyGzrr7nsJ5` · nan

## The plant kingdom: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

- At least some parts of any plant are green, caused by the presence of the pigment **chlorophyll** which absorbs energy from sunlight for the process of **photosynthesis**
- The plant kingdom includes organisms such as **ferns and flowering plants**

#### Ferns

- Have leaves called **fronds**
- Do not produce flowers but instead **reproduce by spores** produced on the underside of fronds

![Diagram of a single green fern frond with many narrow, jagged leaflets arranged alternately along a central stalk on a white background.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/23de929e0ae5-ferns.png)

*Ferns*

![Diagram of a green fern frond showing rows of orange reproductive spores on the underside, with a label indicating “reproductive spores”.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/63dfc0e074c9-ferns-reproduce-by-spores-found-on-the-underside.png)

*Ferns reproduce by spores found on the underside of their fronds*

#### Flowering plants

- Reproduce sexually by means of **flowers and seeds**
- Seeds are produced inside the ovary found at the base of the flower
- Can be divided into two groups – **monocotyledons** and **dicotyledons**

![Simplified colour illustration of golden wheat ears with overlapping grain seeds and thin awns on a white background, labelled by Save My Exams](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/019eb6c102af-wheat-plants-are-monocotyledons.png)

*Wheat plants are monocotyledons*

![Simple illustration of a bright yellow sunflower with layered petals, a brown centre and a straight green stem on a plain white background](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/65988b4556e0-sunflowers-are-dicotyledons.png)

*Sunflowers are dicotyledons*

#### How do you distinguish between monocotyledons and dicotyledons?

- **Flowers**

  - Flowers from** monocotyledons** contain petals in **multiples of three **while flowers from** **dicotyledons contain petals in **multiples of four or five**

- **Leaves**

  - Leaves from monocotyledons have **parallel leaf veins **while leaves from dicotyledons have **reticulated leaf veins**
  
    - Reticulated means the veins form a web-like network throughout the leaf
  - Leaves from monocotyledons are **narrow **and grass-like while leaves from dicotyledons tend to have **broader** leaves that come in a wide range of shapes

![Diagram comparing monocot and dicot plants, showing roots, flowers and leaves, with labels for petal, flower parts, midrib, parallel and reticulated veins.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/797b362ab0c0-comparing-monocots-and-dicots.png)

*Comparing monocots and dicots*

> **Exam Hint**
> Identification of monocotyledons and dicotyledons comes up fairly frequently in both the multiple choice paper and theory paper, and so it is worth learning the differences between their flowers and leaves outlined above.

## Viruses: Extended

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_CXZS5kt77mNnJ6pt` · nan

## Viruses: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

- Viruses are not part of any classification system as they are **not considered living organisms**

  - They **do not carry out the seven life processes** for themselves, instead they **take over a host cell’s metabolic pathways** in order to make multiple copies of themselves
- Virus structure is simply **genetic material** (either RNA or DNA) inside a **protein coat**

![Diagram of a virus showing labelled DNA or RNA strand in the centre, surrounded by a protein coat and an outer envelope.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/a3271360a425-structure-of-a-typical-virus.png)

*Structure of a typical virus*

title: Cell Structure
bodyMd:
# Cell Structure ## Animal & plant cells > **Spec point** — `2.1.1` · Describe and compare the structure of a plant cell with an animal cell, limited to: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, chloroplasts, ribosomes, mitochondria, vacuoles ## Animal & plant cells ### Animal cell structure - **The main features of animal cells:** - they contain a **nucleus** with a **distinct membrane** - **cells do not** have **cellulose cell walls** - their cells **do not** contain **chloroplasts** (so they **are unable** to carry out **photosynthesis**) - they contain carbohydrates stored as **glycogen** #### Animal cell diagram ![Diagram of a typical animal cell labelled with cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes on rough endoplasmic reticulum](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/6336e7621ab4-a-typical-animal-cell.png) *A typical animal cell* ### Plant cell structure - **The main features of plant cells:** - they contain a **nucleus** with a **distinct membrane** - cells have **cell walls** made out of **cellulose** - they contain **chloroplasts** (so they can carry out **photosynthesis**) - carbohydrates are stored as **starch** or **sucrose** #### Plant cell diagram ![Diagram of a typical plant cell labelled with cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria, rough ER, ribosomes and vacuole](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/bf31e104ae8e-a-typical-plant-cells.png) *A typical plant cell* ### Animal and plant cell structure and function table | **Structure** | **Function** | |---|---| | Nucleus | - Contains the DNA (genetic material) which controls the activities of the cell | | Cytoplasm | - A gel like substance composed of water and **dissolved solutes**
- Supports the internal structures of the cell
- Site of many **chemical reactions** (including anaerobic respiration) | | Cell membrane | - Holds the cell together separating the inside of the cell from the outside
- Controls which substances** enter or leave** the cell | | Ribosomes | - Found in the cytoplasm
- The site of **protein synthesis** | | Mitochondria | - The site of **aerobic respiration** | ### Cell structure diagram ![Diagram comparing animal and plant cells as they would look observed with a light microscope, labelling nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane in both, plus cell wall, permanent vacuole and chloroplasts in plant cell](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/f92db9cc805d-an-animal-and-plant-cell-as-seen-under-a-light-m.png) *An animal and plant cell as seen under a light microscope* ### Additional plant cell structure and function table | **Structure** | **Function** | |---|---| | Cell wall | - Made of **cellulose **(a polymer of glucose)
- Gives the cell extra **support**, defining its shape | | Chloroplast | - Contains the green **chlorophyll **pigment that absorbs light energy for **photosynthesis** | | Permanent vacuole | - Contains **cell sap**: a solution of sugar and salt
- Used for storage of certain materials
- Helps to **support **the shape of the cell | ## Bacteria cells > **Spec point** — `2.1.1` · Describe the structure of a bacterial cell, limited to: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA, plasmids ## Bacteria cells ### Bacteria cell structure - Bacteria, which have a wide variety of shapes and sizes, all share the following biological characteristics: - they are **microscopic single-celled organisms** - possess a **cell wall** (made of **peptidoglycan**, not cellulose), **cell membrane**, **cytoplasm** and **ribosomes** - **lack a nucleus** but contain a **circular chromosome of DNA that floats in the cytoplasm** - ***plasmids*** are sometimes present - these are **small rings of DNA** (also floating in the cytoplasm) that contain **extra genes** to those found in the chromosomal DNA - they** lack mitochondria, chloroplasts and other membrane-bound organelles** found in animal and plant cells - Some bacteria also have a **flagellum** (singular) or **several flagella** (plural). These are **long, thin, whip-like tails** attached to bacteria that allow them to **move** - Examples of bacteria include: - ***Lactobacillus*** (a rod-shaped bacterium used in the production of yoghurt from milk) - ***Pneumococcus*** (a spherical bacterium that acts as the pathogen causing pneumonia) #### Bacteria cell diagram ![Diagram of a typical bacterial cell labelled with cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA loop and plasmids](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/1ea0a4eb3551-a-typical-bacterial-cell.png) *A typical bacterial cell* ## Identifying cell structures & function > **Spec point** — `2.1.1` · Identify the cell structures listed in diagrams and images of plant, animal and bacterial cells Describe the functions of the structures in plant, animal and bacterial cells ## Identifying cell structures & function - Within the cytoplasm, the following organelles are visible in almost all cells except prokaryotes when looking at higher magnification (ie using an electron microscope): - **mitochondria** (singular: mitochondrion) are organelles found throughout the cytoplasm - **ribosomes** are tiny structures that can be free within the cytoplasm or attached to a system of membranes within the cell known as **endoplasmic reticulum** - Endoplasmic reticulum studded with ribosomes looks **rough** under the microscope; this gives rise to its name of **rough endoplasmic reticulum** (often shortened to **R.E.R.**) - **vesicles** can also be seen using a higher magnification - these are small circular structures found moving throughout the cytoplasm ### Identifying cell structures under a microscope ![Diagram comparing organelles in animal cells seen with light and electron microscopes, labelling structures visible with both microscopes, nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm and additional structures visible with an electron microscope, ribosomes and mitochondria](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/dddc4a1aa643-structures-in-an-animal-cell-visible-under-a-lig.png) *Structures in an animal cell visible under a light microscope and an electron microscope* ![Diagram comparing plant cells under light and electron microscopes, labelling cell membrane, cell wall, vacuole, cytoplasm and chloroplasts (structures visible with both microscopes), and mitochondria and ribosomes (structures visible with an electron micropscope)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/664d9a84e5cb-structures-in-a-plant-cell-visible-under-a-light.png) *Structures in a plant cell visible under a light microscope and an electron microscope*

title: Organisation of Cells
bodyMd:
# Organisation of Cells ## Producing new cells > **Spec point** — `2.1.2` · State that new cells are produced by division of existing cells ## Producing new cells - The cells in the body need to [divide so that the body can grow and repair](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/17-inheritance/17-1-inheritance-genes-and-cell-division/17-1-6-mitosis/?_ai=internal-linking) itself - Cells grow and divide over and over again - New cells are produced by the **division of existing cells** ## Specialised cells > **Spec point** — `2.1.2` · State that specialised cells have specific functions, limited to: (a) ciliated cells – movement of mucus in the trachea and bronchi (b) root hair cells – absorption (c) palisade mesophyll cells – photosynthesis (d) neurones – conduction of electrical impulses (e) red blood cells – transport of oxygen (f) sperm and egg cells (gametes) – reproduction ## Specialised cells ### Specialised cells in animals and plants - Specialised cells are those which have **developed certain characteristics** in order to **perform particular functions**. These differences are controlled by genes in the nucleus - Cells specialise by undergoing **differentiation**: this is a process by which cells develop the structure and characteristics needed to be able to carry out their functions #### Specialised cells in animals table | Cell | Function | Adaptations | |---|---|---| | Ciliated cell | Movement of mucus in the trachea and bronchi | - Extensions of the cytoplasm at the surface of the cell form hair-like structures called **cilia**, which **beat to move mucus** and trapped particles up to the throat | | Nerve cell | Conduction of impulses | - **Long** so that nerves can run to and from **different parts of the body** to the central nervous system The cell has **extensions and branches** so it can **communicate** with other nerve cells, muscles and glands The axon (extension of cytoplasm away from the cell body) is covered with a **fatty sheath**, which **insulates** the nerve cell and **speeds up** the nerve impulse | | Red blood cell | Transport of oxygen | - **Biconcave disc shape** increases surface area for more efficient diffusion of oxygen Contains **haemoglobin**, which joins with oxygen to transport it Contains **no nucleus**, increasing the amount of space available for haemoglobin inside the cell | | Sperm cell | Reproduction | - The head contains the genetic material for fertilisation in a **haploid nucleus** (containing half the normal number of chromosomes) The **acrosome** in the head contains **digestive enzymes** so that a sperm can penetrate an egg The mid-piece is packed with **mitochondria** to release energy needed to swim and fertilise the egg The **tail** enables the sperm to swim | | Egg cell (ovum) | Reproduction | - Contains a lot of **cytoplasm**, which has **nutrients** for the growth of the early embryo **Haploid nucleus** contains the genetic material for fertilisation Cell membrane **changes after fertilisation** by a single sperm so that **no more sperm can enter** | #### Diagrams of specialised cells in animals ![Diagram of two ciliated epithelial cells showing labelled cilia moving mucus, with labels showing the cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/ceab73557235-ciliated-cells.png) *Ciliated cell* ![Diagram of a motor neurone showing the dendrites, cell body with nucleus and ribosomes, axon with myelin sheath and cytoplasm, and a branched nerve ending](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/f04af17fc585-nerve-cell.png) *Nerve cell* ![Diagram of two red blood cells showing their characteristic biconcave shape without nucleus, cytoplasm containing haemoglobin and the cell membrane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/d94e61856f29-red-blood-cells.png) *Red blood cells* ![Diagram of a human sperm cell labelled with head containing the acrosome and the nucleus, the mitochondria in the mid-piece, and the long tail or flagellum. The cytoplasm and cell membrane (present throughout) are also labelled.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/969ae6d5c3a0-sperm-cell.png) *Sperm cell* ![Diagram of a human egg cell labelled with follicle cells, zona pellucida, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and yolk droplets](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/adc50bae3581-egg-cell.png) *Egg cell* #### Specialised cells in plants table | Cell | Function | Adaptations | |---|---|---| | Root hair cell | Absorption of water and mineral ions from soil | - Root hair increases surface area of the cell to ensure maximum absorption of water and mineral ions
- Walls are thin to ensure water moves through quickly
- No chloroplasts present | | Xylem vessel | Conduction of water through the plant, support of the plant | - No top and bottom walls between xylem vessels, so there is a continuous column of water running through them
- Cells are dead and lack organelles and cytoplasm, allowing free passage of water
- Walls are thickened with a substance called lignin, which provides additional structural support to the plant | | Palisade mesophyll cell | Photosynthesis | - Column-shaped to maximise absorption of sunlight and to allow as many cells as possible to fit in a layer under the upper epidermis of the leaf
- Packed with chloroplasts for maximum photosynthesis | #### Diagrams of specialised cells in plants ![Diagram of a plant root hair cell labelled with cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, vacuole, nucleus, mitochondrion, ribosomes and the root hair extension](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/a9c4bafbb258-root-hair-cell.png) *Root hair cell* ![Diagram of a xylem vessel showing lignin-thickened walls, hollow dead cells formed from broken-down cell walls which contain no typical cell structures , forming a continuous water column.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/3da40478302e-xylem-structure.png) *Xylem structure* ![Diagram of a palisade mesophyll cell showing the cell wall, cytoplasm, nucleus, ribosomes, chloroplasts, mitochondria and a large central vacuole](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/782264c8f8aa-palisade-mesophyll-cell.png) *Palisade mesophyll cell* ## Levels of organisation in an organism > **Spec point** — `2.1.2` · Describe the meaning of the terms: cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism as illustrated by examples given in the syllabus ## Levels of organisation in an organism | Level | Description | |---|---| | Cells | Basic functional and structural units of all living organisms | | Tissues | Groups of cells of similar structure working together to perform the same function | | Organs | Made from different tissues working together to perform specific functions | | Organ systems | Groups of organs with related functions, working together to perform body functions | ![Diagram showing biological organisation as exemplified by a heart muscle cell, heart muscle tissue, the heart organ, circulatory system in a deer, then the whole deer organism.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/231366d4a105-levels-of-organisation.png) *Levels of organisation* ### Examples of systems in animals and plants | System | Organs | Tissue examples | |---|---|---| | Digestive system | - Oesophagus

title: Magnification Formula
bodyMd:
# Magnification Formula

## Magnification formula

> **Spec point** — `2.1.3` · State and use the formula: magnification = image size ÷ actual size
Calculate magnification and size of biological specimens using millimetres as units

## Magnification formula

### Calculating magnification and specimen size using millimetres as units

- Magnification is calculated using the following formula:

**Magnification = Image size ÷ Actual size**

- A better way to remember the formula is using a formula triangle

![Magnification formula triangle showing I above A and M, with text explaining I = image size, A = actual size, M = magnification](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/31f280b4b7df-magnification-equation.png)

*Magnification formula triangle*

- Rearranging the formula to find things other than magnification becomes easy when using the triangle. Whatever value is unknown gets covered with a finger, and whatever is left is what gets calculated:

  - Magnification = image size ÷ actual size
  - Actual size = image size ÷ magnification
  - Image size = magnification × actual size

Remember magnification does not have any units and is just written as ‘x 10’ or ‘x 5000’

> **Worked Example**
> An image of an animal cell is 30 mm in size and it has been magnified by a factor of x 3000. What is the actual size of the cell?
> 
> To find the actual size of the cell:
> 
> ![Diagram showing the magnification formula triangle, with A (actual size) covered by a finger, leaving  I (image size) over M (magnification) and the  worked example showing that in this example,  A = I ÷ M = 30 mm ÷ 3000 = 0.01 mm = 10 μm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/a9d8883434d4-worked-example-using-magnification-equation.png)
> 
> *Worked example using the magnification formula triangle*

> **Exam Hint**
> This skill most frequently comes up in paper 5 and 6 (although it also comes up in the multiple choice and occasionally the theory paper) and you will definitely have to **calculate either magnification, drawing size or actual size** in a least one paper. To ensure you are awarded marks:
> 
> 1. Always **look at the units** that have been given in the question - if you are asked to measure something, most often you will be expected to measure it in millimetres NOT in centimetres - double check the question to see!
> 2. **Learn the equation triangle for magnification** and write it on the page straight away
> 3. Don’t forget that **magnification has NO UNITS** - students often lose a mark because they put one in

title: Converting Between Units
bodyMd:
# Converting Between Units

## Converting between units: Extended

> **Spec point** — `2.1.4` · Convert measurements between millimetres (mm) and micrometres (μm)

## Converting between units: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

#### Using millimetres and micrometres as units

- The table below shows how millimetres are related to two other measures of length

| Unit | Length in mm |
|---|---|
| 1 centimetre (**cm**) | 10 |
| 1 millimetre (**mm**) | 1 |
| 1 micrometre (**μm)** | 0.001 |

- What this basically means is that 1 mm = 1000 µm and 1 cm = 10 000µm
- Unit conversion is necessary in calculation questions where two values are given in different units. Both need converting into the same unit before the calculation can be carried out

> **Worked Example**
> ![Biology exam diagram of leaf cross-section with question about magnification; the leaf has a thickness of 2000 µm and the image size is 50 mm, four answers shown with option B, ×25, circled as correct](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/67330223f04a-example-extended-magnification-question.png)
> 
> - Both values (2000 μm and 50 mm) have different units, so one value needs to be converted so that they have the same units
> 
>   - It doesn't matter which value is converted
> - 2000 μm can be converted into 50 mm
> 
>   - Remember 1000 µm = 1 mm, so divide 2000 by 1000 to convert the leaf thickness from μm into mm
>   - 2000 / 1000 = 2
>   - So the actual thickness of the leaf is 2 mm and the drawing thickness is 50 mm
> 
> - Magnification = image size / actual size = 50 / 2 = 25
> - So the correct answer is a magnification is **x 25**
> 
>   - Remember there are no units for magnification!

> **Exam Hint**
> If you are given a question with two different units in it, make sure you convert them to the same unit before doing your calculation. If you don’t there is a good chance that your answer will be the same as one of the incorrect options in a multiple choice question so you may think you got it correct when, in fact, you haven’t!
> 
> The following diagram may help with unit conversion between mm and µm:
> 
> ![Diagram showing 1 mm equals 1000 micrometres, with arrows: multiply by 1000 to convert mm to µm and divide by 1000 to convert µm to mm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/60b245702dc0-converting-units.png)
> 
> *Converting units between millimetres and micrometres*

title: Diffusion in Biology
bodyMd:
# Diffusion in Biology ## Diffusion > **Spec point** — `3.1.1` · nan ## Diffusion ### What is diffusion in biology? - Diffusion is the **movement of molecules** from a region of its **higher** concentration to a region of its **lower** concentration - Molecules **move down a concentration gradient**, as a result of their **random movement** ![Diagram of passive diffusion: molecules move from higher to lower concentration across a cell membrane’s lipid bilayer, from extracellular fluid to cytoplasm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/98cfb3d93dee-diffusion-across-the-cell-membrane.png) *Diffusion across the cell membrane* - For **living cells**, the principle of the movement down a concentration gradient is the same, but the cell is surrounded by a **cell membrane** which can **restrict the free movement of the molecules** - The cell membrane is a **partially permeable membrane** - this means it allows some molecules to cross easily, but others with difficulty or not at all - The simplest sort of selection is based on the size of the molecules - Diffusion helps living organisms to: - Obtain many of their **requirements** - Get rid of many of their **waste products** - Carry out **gas exchange for respiration** ### Examples of diffusion in living organisms - Living organisms obtain **various substances** they need through **diffusion**, such as **oxygen**, **carbon dioxide**, and other **nutrients**. - It is worth noting that plants require **oxygen** for **respiration** at all times, as well as **carbon dioxide** for **photosynthesis** when conditions for photosynthesis are right (e.g. enough light and a suitable temperature) #### Examples of diffusion in living organisms | Site | Molecules moving | From | To | |---|---|---|---| | Small intestine | Digested food products:

- Glucose
- Amino acids
- Fatty acids
- Glycerol | Lumen of the small intestine | Blood / lymph in villi covering the wall of the small intestine | | Leaf | Oxygen | Air spaces between mesophyll cells | Mitochondria in all cells | | Leaf | Carbon dioxide | Air spaces between mesophyll cells | Chloroplasts in mesophyll cells | | Leaf | Water vapour | Stomatal pores | Air outside stomata | | Lungs | Oxygen | Alveolar air space | Blood in capillaries around alveoli | | Lungs | Carbon dioxide | Blood in capillaries around alveoli | Alveolar air space | ### Where does the energy for diffusion come from? - All particles move randomly at all times - This is known as Brownian motion - The energy for diffusion comes from the kinetic energy of this random movement of molecules and ions ![Diagram of a closed beaker containing many randomly spaced, moving gas molecules, shown as purple circles with motion lines and labelled “gas molecules”, illustrating Brownian motion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/c5fd69bee297-brownian-motion.png) *Brownian motion*

title: Factors that Influence Diffusion
bodyMd:
# Factors that Influence Diffusion

## Factors that influence diffusion

> **Spec point** — `3.1.2` · Investigate the factors that influence diffusion, limited to: surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance

## Factors that influence diffusion

### Surface area to volume ratio

- The **bigger** a cell or structure is, the **smaller its surface area to volume ratio** is, slowing down the rate at which substances can move across its surface

  - Bigger structures have proportionally less surface area relative to their volume, which limits diffusion efficiency
- Many cells which are adapted for diffusion have **increased surface area** in some way, for example:

  - root hair cells in plants (which absorb water and mineral ions)
  - cells lining the ileum in animals (which absorb the products of digestion)

![Diagram showing adaptations of a plant root hair cell and an animal intestinal epithelial cell, both with folded membranes increasing surface area for water and food absorption.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/1eaecdb9cede-cell-adaptations-for-diffusion.png)

*Cell adaptations for diffusion *

![Diagram of the small intestine wall showing finger-like villi with blood capillaries, illustrating a large surface area for efficient nutrient absorption by diffusion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/2933c97f634a-the-highly-folded-surface-of-the-small-intestine.png)

*The highly folded surface of the small intestine increases its surface area*

### Distance

- The smaller the distance molecules have to travel, the higher the rate at which diffusion can occur
- This is why blood capillaries and alveoli have walls which are only one cell thick, to ensure the rate of diffusion across them is as high as possible

### Temperature

- The higher the temperature, the faster molecules move as they have more kinetic energy
- There is therefore a faster net rate of diffusion of molecules from a high to low concentration at higher temperatures

### Concentration gradient

- The greater the difference in concentration on either side of the membrane, the greater the rate of diffusion
- This is because there are more molecules on the higher-concentration side, so more molecules move from high to low concentration by random motion than move from low to high - giving a faster **net** rate of diffusion in that direction

> **Exam Hint**
> You should have carried out investigations into the factors that influence the rate of diffusion and as so should be able to use the information above to **explain experimental results** in an exam. You should also be able to **plan and carry out an experiment** which can investigate the effect of one of these factors.

title: Water
bodyMd:
# Water

## Water as a solvent

> **Spec point** — `3.1.3` · Describe the role of water as a solvent in organisms with reference to digestion, excretion and transport

## Water as a solvent

- Water is important for all living organisms as **many substances are able to dissolve in it** (it is a **solvent**)
- This makes it incredibly useful and essential for all life on Earth
- Water is important as a solvent in the following situations within organisms:

  - Dissolved substances can be **easily transported** around organisms - eg [xylem and phloem of plants](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/8-transport-in-plants/8-1-transport-in-plants/8-1-1-xylem-and-phloem/?_ai=internal-linking) and dissolved food molecules in the blood
  - **Digested food molecules** are in the alimentary canal but need to be **moved to cells** all over the body - without water as a solvent this would not be able to happen
  - Toxic substances such as **urea** and substances in excess of requirements such as **salts** can dissolve in water which makes them easy to **remove from the body in urine**
  - Water is also an important part of the **cytoplasm** and plays a role in ensuring **metabolic reactions can happen** as necessary in cells

![Diagram showing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions surrounded by polar water molecules and a beaker with dissolved Na⁺ and Cl⁻, illustrating salt (a solute) dissolving in water (a solvent)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/17f6db455888-water-as-a-solvent.png)

*Water as a solvent*

title: Osmosis
bodyMd:
# Osmosis

## Osmosis

> **Spec point** — `3.1.4` · State that water diffuses through partially permeable membranes by osmosis
State that water moves into and out of cells by osmosis through the cell membrane

## Osmosis

- All cells are surrounded by a cell membrane which is **partially permeable**
- **Water** can move in and out of cells across the cell membrane by osmosis
- Osmosis is the diffusion of water molecules from a **dilute solution** (low solute concentration) to a **more concentrated solution** (high solute concentration) across a **partially permeable membrane**

  - The cell membrane is partially permeable which means it allows **small molecules** (like water) through but not larger molecules (like solute molecules)
- In doing this, water is moving down the **concentration gradient from where there is more water to where there is less**

![Diagram illustrating how osmosis occurs by showing a partially permeable membrane which has pores that allow small water molecules to pass through which larger solute molecules cannot.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/30015d22251f-osmosis-and-the-partially-permeable-membrane.png)

*Osmosis and the partially permeable membrane*

> **Exam Hint**
> If you are taking the extended exam papers, you should be able to explain the process of osmosis with reference to water potential gradients, as detailed in the revision note page titled ['Osmosis in Animals & Plants'](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/3-movement-into-and-out-of-cells/3-1-diffusion-osmosis-and-active-transport/3-1-6-osmosis-in-animals-and-plants/).

title: Osmosis Experiments
bodyMd:
# Osmosis Experiments

## Osmosis experiments

> **Spec point** — `3.1.5` · Investigate osmosis using materials such as dialysis tubing
Investigate and describe the effects on plant tissues of immersing them in solutions of different concentrations

## Osmosis experiments

### Immersing plant cells in solutions of different concentrations

- The most common osmosis practical involves cutting **cylinders of root vegetables** such as potato or radish and placing them into **distilled water** and **sucrose solutions** of increasing concentration
- The cylinders are weighed before placing into the solutions
- They are left in the solutions for 20 - 30 minutes and then removed, dried to remove excess liquid and reweighed

![Diagram illustrating how the mass of two individual radish pieces of almost equal initial size changes after they have been placed into two different solutions (one in a dilute sugar solution and the other in a concentrated sugar solution for 4 hours). The radish in the dilute solution has increased in mass and length as a result of water moving into the radish by osmosis, in contrast to the other radish piece which has decreased in mass and length after being placed in the more concentrated sugar solution.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/d3fe2221b613-osmosis-in-plant-tissue.png)

*Potatoes are usually used in osmosis experiments to show how the concentration of a solution affects the movement of water, but radishes can be used too*

- If the plant tissue gains mass:

  - Water must have moved into the plant tissue from the solution surrounding it by osmosis
  - The solution surrounding the tissue is more dilute than the plant tissue (which is more concentrated)
- If plant tissue loses mass:

  - Water must have moved out of the plant tissue into the solution surrounding it by osmosis
  - The solution surrounding the tissue is more concentrated than the plant tissue (which is more dilute)
- If there is no overall change in mass:

  - There has been no **net** movement of water as the concentration in both the plant tissue and the solution surrounding it must be equal
  - Water is still moving into and out of the tissue - it's just that the movement in each direction is balanced, so there's no overall change

### Investigating osmosis using dialysis tubing

- **Dialysis tubing** (sometimes referred to as Visking tubing) is a non-living **partially permeable** membrane made from cellulose
- Pores in this membrane are small enough to **prevent the passage of large molecules** (such as **sucrose**) but allow **smaller molecules** (such as **glucose and water**) to pass through by **diffusion **and **osmosis**
- This can be demonstrated by:

  - filling a section of dialysis tubing with concentrated sucrose solution
  - suspending the tubing in a boiling tube of water for a set period of time
  - noting whether the water level outside the tubing decreases as water moves into the tubing via osmosis
- Water moves from a region of [higher water potential](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/3-movement-into-and-out-of-cells/3-1-diffusion-osmosis-and-active-transport/3-1-6-osmosis-in-animals-and-plants/?_ai=internal-linking) (dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated solution), through a partially permeable membrane

![Diagram of a visking tubing bag filled with sucrose solution, tied at both ends and immersed in distilled water in a beaker, illustrating osmosis.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/ad30b88177fe-visking-tubing-2.png)

*An example setup of a dialysis tubing experiment*

title: Osmosis in Animals & Plants
bodyMd:
# Osmosis in Animals & Plants

## Osmosis in plant tissues

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_FVz2QYpwRd5bKWfx`

## Osmosis in plant tissues

- When water moves into a plant cell, the vacuole gets bigger, **pushing the cell membrane against the cell wall**
- Water entering the cell by osmosis makes the cell **rigid and firm**
- This is important for plants as the effect of all the cells in a plant being firm is to **provide support and strength for the plant** - making the plant stand upright with its leaves held out to catch sunlight
- The pressure created by the **cell wall** stops too much water entering and **prevents the cell from bursting**
- If plants do not receive enough water the cells cannot remain rigid and firm (turgid) and the plant **wilts**

## Osmosis: Extended

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_VCWcZxVHZqTfWqTZ`

## Osmosis: Extended

- Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of **higher water potential** (dilute solution) to a region of **lower water potential** (concentrated solution), through a **partially permeable membrane**
- **To understand this topic with clarity, it is important to understand the following:**

  - High water potential = dilute solution = low solute concentration (right side of diagram)
  - Low water potential = concentrated solution = high solute concentration (left side of diagram)

> **Exam Hint**
> The best explanations to do with osmosis will refer to **water potential**, so if you are aiming for an A* or A grade (or a grade 7, 8 or 9) you will need to understand the concept and use it in your explanations.

## Osmosis in animals & plants: Extended

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_mpCWHqP24s9pMgwG` · Explain the effects on plant cells of immersing them in solutions of different concentrations by using the terms: turgid, turgor pressure, plasmolysis, flaccid
Explain the importance of water potential and osmosis in the uptake and loss of water by organisms

## Osmosis in animals & plants: Extended

### Plant cells in solutions of different concentrations

- When plant cells are placed in a solution that has a **higher water potential** (dilute solution) than inside the cells (e.g. distilled water) then water moves into the plant cells via osmosis
- These water molecules push the cell membrane against the cell wall, increasing the **turgor pressure** in the cells which makes them **turgid**

![Diagram of a turgid plant cell showing thick cell wall, full central vacuole, nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/840c431e8c9d-a-turgid-plant-cell.png)

*A turgid plant cell*

- When plant cells are placed in a **concentrated** solution (with a lower water potential than inside the cells) water molecules will move **out of the plant cells by osmosis**, making them flaccid

  - If plant cells become flaccid it can negatively affect the plant's ability to support itself
- If looked at underneath the microscope, the plant cells might be **plasmolysed**, meaning the cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall

![Diagram of a plasmolysed plant cell showing shrunken cytoplasm and vacuole pulled from the rigid cell wall, with chloroplasts and organelles around the edge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/df416fd7f98b-a-plasmolysed-plant-cell.png)

*A plasmolysed plant cell*

### Animal cells in solutions of different concentrations

- **Animal cells** also lose and gain water as a result of osmosis
- As animal cells **do not have a supporting cell wall**, the results on the cell are more severe
- If an animal cell is placed into a **strong sugar solution** (with a lower water potential than the cell), it will lose water by osmosis and become **crenated** (shrivelled up)
- If an animal cell is placed into **distilled water** (with a higher water potential than the cell), it will gain water by osmosis and, as it has **no cell wall to create turgor pressure**, will continue to do so until the cell membrane is stretched too far and **it bursts**

![Diagram comparing red blood cells in hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic solutions, showing water movement by osmosis causing shrivelled cells in a hypertonic solution,  normal cells in an isotonic solution and swollen and lysed cells in the hypotonic solution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/c88edc9bf557-effect-of-osmosis-on-animal-cells.png)

*Effect of osmosis on animal cells*

# Active Transport

## Active transport

> **Spec point** — `3.3.1` · Describe active transport as the movement of particles through a cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration (i.e. against a concentration gradient), using energy from respiration

## Active transport

- Active transport is the movement of particles through a cell membrane from a region of **lower concentration** to a region of **higher concentration** using [energy from respiration](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/12-respiration/12-1-respiration/12-1-1-respiration-in-cells/?_ai=internal-linking)

![Diagram of active transport: carrier proteins move particles across a cell membrane from low concentration outside the cell to higher concentration inside.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/58cacb6d7c54-active-transport-across-the-cell-membrane.png)

title: Proteins & Active Transport
bodyMd:
# Proteins & Active Transport

## Importance of active transport: Extended

> **Spec point** — `3.3.2` · Explain the importance of active transport as a process for movement of molecules or ions across membranes, including ion uptake by root hairs

## Importance of active transport: Extended

- Energy is needed because particles are being moved **against a concentration gradient**, in the opposite direction from which they would naturally move ([by diffusion](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/3-movement-into-and-out-of-cells/3-1-diffusion-osmosis-and-active-transport/3-1-1-diffusion-in-biology/?_ai=internal-linking))
- Active transport is vital process for the movement of molecules or ions across membranes
- Including:

  - **uptake of glucose** by epithelial cells in the [villi of the small intestine](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/biology/cie/23/revision-notes/7-human-nutrition/7-1-human-diet-and-digestion/7-1-14-adaptations-of-the-small-intestine/?_ai=internal-linking) and by kidney tubules in the nephron
  - **uptake of ions** from soil water by root hair cells in plants

## Protein carriers: Extended

> **Spec point** — `3.3.3` · State that protein carriers move molecules or ions across a membrane during active transport

## Protein carriers: Extended

- Active transport works by using **carrier proteins** embedded in the cell membrane to pick up specific molecules and take them through the cell membrane against their concentration gradient:

1. Substance combines with carrier protein molecule in the cell membrane
2. Carrier transports substances across membrane using energy from respiration to give them the kinetic energy needed to change shape and move the substance through the cell membrane
3. Substance released into cell

![Diagram of active transport: carrier proteins in a cell membrane move particles into the cell from lower to higher concentration against the gradient.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/90f758cf13f8-26212-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads20251036598.png)

*Carrier proteins in active transport*

> **Exam Hint**
> You don't need to know anything about the phospholipid bilayer when it comes to active transport!

title: Chemicals & Life
bodyMd:
# Chemicals & Life ## Chemical elements > **Spec point** — `4.1.1` · List the chemical elements that make up: carbohydrates, fats and proteins ## Chemical elements - Most of the molecules in living organisms fall into three categories: **carbohydrates, proteins and lipids** - These **all contain carbon** and so are described as organic molecules ### Chemical elements table | Molecule | Chemical elements | |---|---| | Carbohydrate | - Carbon (C)
- Oxygen (O)
- Hydrogen (H) | | Protein | All contain:

- Carbon (C)
- Oxygen (O)
- Hydrogen (H)
- Nitrogen (N)

Some contain small amounts of other elements, for example:

- Sulfur (S)
- Selenium (Se) | | Lipid | - Carbon (C)
- Oxygen (O)
- Hydrogen (H) | ## Large molecules are made from smaller molecules > **Spec point** — `4.1.1` · State that large molecules are made from smaller molecules, limited to: (a) starch, glycogen and cellulose from glucose (b) proteins from amino acids (c) fats and oils from fatty acids and glycerol ## Large molecules are made from smaller molecules ### Carbohydrates - Long chains of **simple sugars **(monosaccharides) - **Glucose** is a simple sugar - When **two glucose molecules join together maltose is formed** (a disaccharide) - When **lots** of glucose molecules join together **starch, glycogen or cellulose** can form (a polysaccharide) ![Diagram showing three carbohydrates (all long chains of glucose molecules joined together) in cells: animal cells (exemplified by a liver cell) storing glycogen in glycogen granules and plant cells (exemplified by a palisade mesophyll cell) storing starch in starch grains in the chloroplasts and cellulose used in the cell wall .](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/c3e6654d19aa-glycogen-cellulose-and-starch-are-all-made-from-.png) *Glycogen, cellulose and starch are all made from glucose molecules* ### Fats - Most fats (lipids) in the body are made up of **triglycerides** - Their basic unit is **one glycerol molecule chemically bonded to three fatty acid chains** - The fatty acids vary in size and structure - Lipids are divided into **fats** (solids at room temperature) and **oils** (liquids at room temperature) ![Diagram of a triglyceride showing a vertical glycerol backbone joined to three long hydrocarbon fatty acid tails.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/c947fd487b4b-structure-of-a-triglyceride.png) *Structure of a triglyceride* ### Proteins - Long chains of **amino acids** - There are about 20 different amino acids - They all contain the **same basic structure** but the **‘R’ group is different for each one** - When amino acids are joined together a protein is formed - The amino acids can be arranged in any order, resulting in hundreds of thousands of different proteins - Even a small difference in the order of the amino acids results in a different protein being formed ![Diagram of the general amino acid structure showing a central carbon with four chemical bonds, one with an NH₂ amino group to the left, H above, a COOH carboxyl group to the right and R group to the bottom.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/50efd037f9c9-general-amino-acid-structure.png) *General amino acid structure* ![Diagram showing separate coloured circles representing individual amino acids, coloured circles attached to each other representing amino acids joined together to form a peptide chain, and finally a long peptide chain folded into a complex protein, titled “How your body uses amino acids”.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/b025a52291a9-amino-acids-join-together-to-form-proteins.png) *Amino acids join together to form proteins*
