bodyMd:
# Food Tests

## Food tests

> **Spec point** — `4.1.2` · Describe the use of:
(a) iodine solution test for starch
(b) Benedict’s solution test for reducing sugars
(c) biuret test for proteins
(d) ethanol emulsion test for fats and oils
(e) DCPIP test for vitamin C

## Food tests

### Food test for glucose (a reducing sugar)

- Add **Benedict's solution** into sample solution in test tube
- **Heat** at 80 °C in a water bath for **5 minutes**
- Take test tube out of water bath and observe the colour
- A positive test will show a colour change from **blue to orange or brick red**

![Diagram of Benedict's test for sugars. A test tube with solution and Benedict's solution is heated in a water bath over a flame to observe colour change.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/1950b88b11af-the-benedicts-test-for-glucose.png)

*A positive test for glucose will show a colour change from blue to orange or brick red *

<u>[Use this image](https://www.savemyexams.com/info/policies/using-our-illustrations-images-fair-use/)</u>

### Food test for starch

- Iodine is used to test for the presence or absence of starch in a food sample

![Diagram showing starch turns blue-black with iodine, maltose doesn't change. Amylase breaks starch into glucose; maltose remains unchanged.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/34a9dbdc146f-the-iodine-test-for-starch.png)

*We can use iodine to test for the presence or absence of starch in a food sample*

<u>[Use this image](https://www.savemyexams.com/info/policies/using-our-illustrations-images-fair-use/)</u>

- Add drops of **iodine solution** to the food sample
- A positive test will show a colour change from **orange-brown to blue-black**

![Steps of a starch test on a potato: whole, peeled, iodine applied turning brown, and colour turns blue-black indicating starch presence.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/df75ea0a23b8-testing-a-potato-to-prove-the-presence-of-starch.png)

*A positive test for starch will show a colour change from orange-brown to blue-black*

<u>[Use this image](https://www.savemyexams.com/info/policies/using-our-illustrations-images-fair-use/)</u>

### Food test for protein

- Add drops of **Biuret solution** to the food sample
- A positive test will show a colour change from **blue to violet / purple**

![Test tubes illustrating a Biuret test. Left tube with Biuret solution drips into food sample, middle shows positive result (purple), right shows negative (blue).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/eb8f9bae95cf-the-biuret-test-for-protein.png)

*A positive test for protein will show a colour change from blue to violet / purple*

[Use this image](https://www.savemyexams.com/info/policies/using-our-illustrations-images-fair-use/)

### Food test for lipids

- Food sample is mixed with **2 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** of ethanol** and shaken
- The ethanol is added to an equal volume of **cold water**
- A positive test will show a **cloudy emulsion** forming

![Four test tubes show ethanol and water mixtures. One is cloudy for a positive emulsion test, and one is clear for a negative result.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/d1029afbf6ff-the-ethanol-test-for-lipids.png)

*A positive test for lipids will show a cloudy emulsion forming*

[Use this image](https://www.savemyexams.com/info/policies/using-our-illustrations-images-fair-use/)

### Food test for vitamin C

- Add **1 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** of DCPIP solution** to a test tube
- Add a small amount of food sample (as a solution)
- A positive test will show the **blue colour of the dye disappearing**

![Pipette adding sample to blue DCPIP in test tube, showing colour change to clear for positive vitamin C test, or remaining blue for negative result.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/c6a6531b8338-63349-dcpip-vit-c-colourless-solution.png)

*A positive test for vitamin C will show the blue colour of the dye disappearing*

<u>[Use this image](https://www.savemyexams.com/info/policies/using-our-illustrations-images-fair-use/)</u>

> **Exam Hint**
> When describing food tests in exam answers, make sure you give the **starting colour** of the solution and **the colour it changes to** for a positive result.

title: DNA Structure
bodyMd:
# DNA Structure

## Structure of a DNA molecule: Extended

> **Spec point** — `4.1.3` · Describe the structure of a DNA molecule:
(a) two strands coiled together to form a double
helix
(b) each strand contains chemicals called bases
(c) bonds between pairs of bases hold the strands together
(d) the bases always pair up in the same way: A with T, and C with G (full names are not required)

## Structure of a DNA molecule: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

- DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, is the molecule that contains the instructions for the growth and development of all organisms
- It consists of two strands of DNA wound around each other in what is called a **double helix**

![Diagram showing DNA double helix forming a DNA strand, packed into a chromosome (with further detail in a label that a chromosome is a long strand of DNA wrapped around proteins) inside the nucleus of a cell with other organelles present (mitochondria, cytoplasm and cell membrane) ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/82b5c2dd0530-dna-chromosomes-and-the-nucleus.png)

*DNA, chromosomes and the nucleus*

- The individual units of DNA are called **nucleotides**

![Diagram of a DNA nucleotide labelled with a phosphate group and deoxyribose sugar which forms the DNA strand backbone, and an attached nitrogenous base A in this image (with a label that the nitrogenous base could be A, T, C or G) ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/201dcf7e54c3-a-nucleotide.png)

*A nucleotide*

- All nucleotides contain the same phosphate and deoxyribose sugar, but differ from each other in the **base** attached
- There are four different bases, **Adenine (A), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T) and Guanine (G)**
- The bases on each strand pair up with each other, holding the two strands of DNA in the double helix
- The bases always pair up in the same way:

  - Adenine always pairs with Thymine **(A-T)**
  - Cytosine always pairs with Guanine **(C-G)**

![Diagram of DNA double helix showing coloured base pairs A–T and C–G joined by hydrogen bonds, and a labelled sugar–phosphate backbone on the outer edge of each strand](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/0f748c670d13-dna-base-pairs.png)

*DNA base pairs*

- The phosphate and sugar section of the nucleotides form the ‘backbone’ of the DNA strand (like the sides of a ladder) and the base pairs of each strand connect to form the rungs of the ladder

![Diagram of DNA showing on the left an unwound DNA double helix, illustrating a sequence of base pairs (with A always paired with T and C paired with G) on two antiparallel strands, and the image on the right shows a double helix, there is a note that genes are sequences of bases, not base pairs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/a5734f79b5e2-the-dna-helix-is-made-from-two-strands-of-dna-he.png)

*The DNA helix is made from two strands of DNA held together by hydrogen bonds*

- It is this sequence of bases that holds the code for the formation of proteins

> **Exam Hint**
> You do not need to learn the names of the bases, **just their letter**. Make sure you **know which bonds with which**, as this is the most commonly asked question about this topic.

title: Enzymes
bodyMd:
# Enzymes

## What are enzymes?

> **Spec point** — `5.1.1` · Describe a catalyst as a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction
Describe enzymes as proteins that are involved in all metabolic reactions, where they function as biological catalysts
Describe why enzymes are important in all living organisms in terms of a reaction rate necessary to sustain life

## What are enzymes?

- Enzymes are:

  - **catalysts** that **speed up** the rate of a chemical reaction **without being changed** or used up in the reaction
  - **proteins**
  - **biological catalysts** (biological because they are **made in living cells**, catalysts because they speed up the rate of chemical reactions without being changed)
  - necessary to all living organisms as they **maintain reaction speeds** of all metabolic reactions (all the reactions that keep an organism alive) at a rate that can **sustain life**
  
    - Without digestive enzymes, one meal would take around 2–3 weeks to digest; with enzymes it takes 3-4 hours

## How do enzymes work?

> **Spec point** — `5.1.1` · Describe enzyme action with reference to the shape of the active site of an enzyme being complementary to its substrate and the formation of products

## How do enzymes work?

![Diagram showing a yellow substrate that has a complementary shape with enzyme 1 on the bottom left but not with enzyme 2 on the bottom right, illustrating complementary active site specificity for enzyme–substrate binding.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/b5323503240c-enzyme-substrate-specificity.png)

*Enzyme substrate specificity*

- Enzymes are **specific** to one particular substrate (molecule/s that get broken down or joined together in the reaction) as the enzyme is a complementary shape to the substrate
- The product is made from the substrate(s) and is released

![Diagram showing the lock-and-key model of enzyme action, from top left labelled 1, where several yellow substrates and purple enzymes are complementary to each other and moving around in solution, bottom left labelled 2 with a single yellow substrate binding at the active site of a purple enzyme to form an enzyme–substrate complex and bottom right the separate products formed from the substate after it had formed a complex with the enzyme. ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/744ab9905a8f-lock-and-key-model-of-enzyme-activity-1.png)

*Enzyme specificity: lock and key model of enzyme activity*

title: Enzyme Investigations
bodyMd:
# Enzyme Investigations

## Investigating the effect of temperature on amylase

> **Spec point** — `5.1.2` · Investigate and describe the effect of changes in temperature and pH on enzyme activity with reference to optimum temperature and denaturation

## Investigating the effect of temperature on amylase

- **Starch solution** is heated to a set temperature
- **Iodine** is added to wells of a spotting tile
- **Amylase** is added to the starch solution and mixed well
- Every minute, droplets of solution are added to a new well of iodine solution
- This is continued until the iodine **stops turning blue-black** (this means there is **no more starch** left in the solution as the amylase has broken it all down)
- Time taken for the reaction to be completed is recorded
- Experiment is repeated at different temperatures
- The quicker the reaction is completed, the faster the enzyme is working

![Diagram of the iodine test method for investigating how temperature affects amylase activity on starch, showing results at 20°C, 40°C, and 60°C.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/a9ece233a12f-investigating-the-effect-of-temperature-on-enzym.png)

*Investigating the effect of temperature on enzyme activity*

## Investigating the effect of pH on amylase

> **Spec point** — `5.1.2` · Investigate and describe the effect of changes in temperature and pH on enzyme activity with reference to optimum temperature and denaturation

## Investigating the effect of pH on amylase

- Place single drops of **iodine** solution in rows on the tile
- Label a test tube with the pH to be tested
- Use the syringe to place 2 cm<sup>3</sup> of **amylase** in the test tube
- Add 1 cm<sup>3</sup> of **buffer solution** to the test tube using a syringe
- Use another test tube to add 2 cm<sup>3</sup> of **starch solution** to the amylase and buffer solution, start the stopwatch whilst mixing using a pipette
- After 10 seconds, use a pipette to place one drop of mixture on the first drop of iodine, which should turn blue-black
- Wait another 10 seconds and place another drop of mixture on the second drop of iodine
- Repeat every 10 seconds **until iodine solution remains orange-brown**
- Repeat experiment at different pH values - the less time the iodine solution takes to remain orange-brown, the quicker all the starch has been digested and so the better the enzyme works at that pH

![Diagram showing step-by-step amylase and starch experiment using iodine on a spotting tile to measure reaction time at different pH buffer solutions (in this case pH 5, pH 7, pH 9 and pH 14.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/6e6d54beecfc-investigating-effect-ph-on-enzyme-activity.png)

*Investigating the effect of pH on enzyme activity*

> **Exam Hint**
> Describing and explaining experimental results for enzyme experiments is a common type of exam question so make sure you understand what is happening and, for the top grades, can relate this to changes in the active site of the enzyme when it has denatured, or if it is a **low temperature**, relate it to the amount of kinetic energy the molecules have.

title: Enzyme Action & Specificity
bodyMd:
# Enzyme Action & Specificity

## Enzyme action & specificity: Extended

> **Spec point** — `5.1.3` · Explain enzyme action with reference to: active site, enzyme-substrate complex, substrate and product
Explain the specificity of enzymes in terms of the complementary shape and fit of the active site with the substrate

## Enzyme action & specificity: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

- Enzymes are **specific** to one particular substrate(s) as the **active site** of the enzyme, where the substrate attaches, is a complementary shape to the substrate
- This is because the enzyme is a protein and has a **specific 3-D shape**
- This is known as the **lock and key hypothesis**
- When the substrate binds with the enzyme's active site, the enzyme and substrate together are known as the **enzyme-substrate complex**
- After the reaction has occurred, the **products** leave the enzyme’s active site as they no longer fit it and it is free to take up another substrate

![Diagram showing the enzyme lock-and-key model: specific substrate fits enzyme 1’s active site, forms complex, is split into products while enzyme remains unchanged](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/524a02d4540b-how-enzymes-work.png)

*How enzymes bind with complementary substrates to break them down/build them up into products*

1. Enzymes and substrates **randomly** move about in solution.

2. When an enzyme and its complementary substrate randomly **collide** - with the substrate fitting into the active site of the enzyme - an **enzyme-substrate complex** forms, and the reaction occurs.

3. A product (or products) forms from the substrate(s) which are then released from the active site. The enzyme is unchanged and will go on to catalyse further reactions.

title: Enzymes & Temperature
bodyMd:
# Enzymes & Temperature

## Enzymes & temperature: Extended

> **Spec point** — `5.1.4` · Explain the effect of changes in temperature on enzyme activity in terms of kinetic energy, shape and fit, frequency of effective collisions and denaturation

## Enzymes & temperature: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

- Enzymes are **proteins** and have a **specific shape**, held in place by **bonds**
- This is extremely important around the **active site** area as the specific shape is what ensures the **substrate will fit into the active site** and enable the reaction to proceed
- Enzymes work fastest at their ‘**optimum temperature**’ – in the human body, the optimum temperature is 37 °C
- Heating to high temperatures (beyond the optimum) **breaks the bonds** that hold the enzyme's structure together, causing it to lose its shape
- This changes the shape of the active site so it's no longer complementary to the substrate, and the enzyme is **denatured**
- Substrates cannot fit into denatured enzymes as the shape of their active site has been lost
- Denaturation is **irreversible** - once enzymes are denatured they cannot regain their proper shape and activity will stop

![Diagram showing how increased temperature denatures an enzyme, distorting its active site so the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme stops working](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/f28c22e8995f-effect-of-temperature-on-enzyme-activity.png)

*Effect of temperature on enzyme activity*

- Increasing the temperature from 0 °C to the optimum increases the activity of enzymes as **the more energy the molecules have the faster they move and the number of collisions with the substrate molecules increases**, leading to a faster rate of reaction
- This means that **low temperatures do not denature enzymes**, they just make them work more slowly

![Graph showing enzyme activity versus temperature, activity rising as temperature increases to an optimum then rapidly falling as enzymes denature, with notes explaining collisions and active site changes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/cc424ec91bd4-graph-showing-the-effect-of-temperature-on-rate-.png)

*Graph showing the effect of temperature on the rate of enzyme activity*

title: Enzymes & pH
bodyMd:
# Enzymes & pH

## Enzymes & pH: Extended

> **Spec point** — `5.1.5` · Explain the effect of changes in pH on enzyme activity in terms of shape and fit and denaturation

## Enzymes & pH: Extended

### Extended Tier Only

- The optimum pH for most enzymes is 7 but some that are produced in acidic conditions, such as the stomach, have a lower optimum pH (pH 2) and some that are produced in alkaline conditions, such as the duodenum, have a higher optimum pH (pH 8 or 9)
- If the pH is too high or too low, the bonds that hold the amino acid chain together to make up the protein can be destroyed
- This will change the shape of the active site, so the substrate can no longer fit into it, reducing the rate of activity
- Moving too far away from the optimum pH will cause the enzyme to denature and activity will stop

![Diagram showing how high pH alters enzyme active site shape so substrate no longer fits, changing from complementary to non-complementary shapes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/73efe9cfa95e-effect-of-ph-on-enzyme-activity.png)

*Effect of pH on enzyme activity*

![Graph of enzyme activity versus pH for an enzyme from the duodenum, showing a peak at optimum pH around 8 and sharp decline at extreme pH above and below pH 8 where enzymes denature and lose activity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/93dea9454620-graph-showing-effect-of-ph-on-rate-of-activity-f.png)

title: Photosynthesis
bodyMd:
# Photosynthesis

## Photosynthesis

> **Spec point** — `6.1.1` · Describe photosynthesis as the process by which plants synthesise carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light

## Photosynthesis

- Green plants make the carbohydrate **glucose** from the raw materials **carbon dioxide** and **water**
- At the same time **oxygen** is made and released as a waste product
- The reaction requires **energy** which is obtained by the pigment **chlorophyll** trapping light from the Sun
- So photosynthesis can be defined as **the process by which plants manufacture carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light**

> **Exam Hint**
> If asked for the raw materials required for photosynthesis, the answer is **carbon dioxide** **and water.**
> 
> Although required for the reaction to take place, light energy is not a substance and therefore cannot be a raw material.

## Photosynthesis word equation

> **Spec point** — `6.1.1` · State the word equation for photosynthesis as: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen in the presence of light and chlorophyll

## Photosynthesis word equation

- The photosynthesis word equation can be summarised as:

$carbon dioxide+water\rightarrow glucose+oxygen_{}$

- The reaction between carbon dioxide and water to form glucose and oxygen occurs **in the presence of light and chlorophyll**

![Diagram showing the word equation for photosynthesis, including how carbon dioxide and water are supplied to the leaf and how glucose and oxygen are used by the plant.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/56161f427df1-how-plants-get-the-materials-they-need.png)

*The inputs, outputs, and requirements of photosynthesis.*

title: Leaf Structure
bodyMd:
# Leaf Structure ## Leaf structure & adaptations for photosynthesis > **Spec point** — `6.1.10` · State that most leaves have a large surface area and are thin, and explain how these features are adaptations for photosynthesis ## Leaf structure & adaptations for photosynthesis ### Leaf structure ![Diagram of a leaf cross‑section labelled with upper and lower epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, vascular bundle, chloroplasts, air spaces and guard cells.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/9a8f88e05909-structure-of-a-leaf-igcse-and-gcse-biology-revis.png) *Diagram showing the cross-section of a leaf* ![Diagram of a leaf cross-section showing CO₂ diffusing through a stoma into spongy mesophyll, then into palisade mesophyll cells and chloroplasts during photosynthesis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-biology-23/assets/b64be45a8089-how-photosynthesising-cells-obtain-carbon-dioxid.png) *How photosynthesising cells obtain carbon dioxide* - Pathway of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to chloroplasts by diffusion: atmosphere → air spaces around spongy mesophyll tissue → leaf mesophyll cells → chloroplast #### Leaf structure table | Structure | Description | |---|---| | Wax cuticle | Protective, waterproof layer on top of the leaf that reduces water loss by evaporation, helping maintain the water needed for photosynthesis | | Upper epidermis | Thin and transparent, allowing light to pass through to the palisade mesophyll beneath | | Palisade mesophyll | Column-shaped cells tightly packed with chloroplasts to absorb as much light as possible, maximising the rate of photosynthesis | | Spongy mesophyll | Contains large air spaces between cells, increasing the surface area available for gas exchange, so carbon dioxide can diffuse quickly to the palisade cells and oxygen can diffuse out | | Lower epidermis | Contains stomata and guard cells, which control gas exchange and water loss (see below) | | Guard cell | Changes shape as it absorbs or loses water, causing the stomata to open or close. This controls the diffusion of carbon dioxide in and oxygen out, and helps regulate water loss | | Stomata (singular: stoma) | - Small pores that allow gas exchange between the leaf and the atmosphere
- Usually open during the day and closed at night, matching when photosynthesis occurs
- Also the main site of water loss by transpiration
- In most plants, found in higher numbers on the lower epidermis to reduce water loss (less exposure to direct sunlight/heat) | | Vascular bundle | Contains xylem and phloem, which transport substances to and from the leaf | | Xylem | Transports water (and dissolved mineral ions) up to the mesophyll cells for use in photosynthesis, and to replace water lost during transpiration | | Phloem | Transports sucrose and amino acids around the plant (translocation), including away from the leaf to where they are needed or stored | #### Adaptations of leaf structure for photosynthesis table | Feature | Adaptation | |---|---| | Large surface area (leaf) | Increases surface area for the diffusion of carbon dioxide and absorption of light for photosynthesis | | Thin | Allows carbon dioxide to diffuse to palisade mesophyll cells quickly | | Chlorophyll | Absorbs light energy so that photosynthesis can take place | | Network of veins | Allows the transports of water to the cells of the leaf for photosynthesis and carbohydrates (as a product of photosynthesis) away from the leaf | | Stomata (singular: stoma) | Allows carbon dioxide to diffuse into the leaf and oxygen to diffuse out | | Epidermis is thin and transparent | Allows as much light as possible to reach the palisade cells | | Thin cuticle made of wax | To protect the leaf without blocking sunlight | | Palisade cell layer (tissue) at the top of leaf | Maximises the absorption of light as it will hit chloroplasts in the cell directly | | Spongy layer | Air spaces allow carbon dioxide to diffuse through the leaf, increasing the surface area | | Vascular bundles | Thick cell walls of the tissue in the bundles help to support the stem and leaf |
